title: shell chemical loss would be buyers gain 2026 09 01
author: Yawen Chen
text:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters Breakingviews) - For Shell (SHEL.L)
, opens new tab
, the chemicals business has swallowed billions in capital but seemingly delivered little in return. CEO Wael Sawan says the assets are good, but also that the UK oil major is ​not their natural owner. A sale therefore makes sense, with the Financial Times recently reporting that ExxonMobil (XOM.N)
, opens new tab
, LyondellBasell (LYB.N)
, opens new tab
, Apollo Global Management (APO.N)
, opens new tab
 and ‌others may be interested in a possible $8 billion deal for the company's U.S. chemicals assets. The twist is that prospective buyers are arriving just as a multi-year industry slump starts to ease.
Petrochemical plants turn inputs such as ethane and naphtha into building blocks like ethylene, which are then used to make plastics and other materials. A few numbers clearly display ​why Shell may be keen to move on. The group's chemicals portfolio had around $25 billion of capital employed in 2024 and generated a ​minus-2% return on that money, the company revealed
, opens new tab
 at a 2025 investor event. Its big Monaca polymers complex in Pennsylvania, ⁠which would be a large part of any possible U.S. asset sale, alone accounted for about $14 billion of the invested capital.
It may be a good ​time to buy, since the industry's backdrop is starting to look less bleak. First, U.S. producers benefit from plentiful domestic ethane, whereas many Asian rivals often ​depend on oil-derived naphtha. The latter has been tricky this year given the disruption in the Middle East, giving American plants like Shell's an advantage. Exxon, for example, said margins in its North American chemicals operations jumped roughly 180% between the first and second quarters. More broadly, prices are higher across the board, which should help all producers: ethylene ​prices in Northeast Asia have rebounded about 30% from their July trough, according to LSEG data.
True, Chinese capacity remains the big structural question for the ​industry. Years of rapid industrial expansion in the People's Republic created chronic oversupply and poor margins in the chemicals business, with spillover effects for the rest of the world. ‌Yet the ⁠Iran shock has forced some Chinese plants to cut production while customers draw down reserves of polymer, which they accumulated during the glut years. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says inventories have fallen significantly. That may admittedly not cure Chinese overcapacity. And a July rebound in imports of ethane and liquefied petroleum gas may suggest that plants in the People's Republic are ramping up again. Still, the future for producers elsewhere at least seems less punishing than the past.
The ​upshot is that Exxon, LyondellBasell, Apollo and ​other possible buyers seem to ⁠have got the timing right. And the price doesn't look crazy, at face value. The FT-reported figure of $8 billion would be less than the $14 billion of capital employed that Shell has tied up in the Monaca plant alone. The ​UK group's reasons for selling are no less valid. The only thing that's changed is that it's now ​easier to imagine why ⁠someone might want to buy.
